_about: Acronyms and names used on the site. term is how it appears; full is the spelled-out name (empty for names that aren't acronyms); meaning is one line. On every page the first use in body text spells the term out as 'full (term)', or the term is wrapped in <Term>; scripts/check-terms.mjs enforces it. Not listed on purpose: part numbers (ESP32, WS2812B, MAX4466, ADALM-PLUTO), the About chip's playful pin names (their notes say what they are), and everyday ones (PDF, LED, USB, LSU, NATO, CDC, CPR, FAQ, QR).

terms.meaning: Cars talking directly to each other by radio.
The short status message (position, speed, heading) a car broadcasts several times a second.
Splits data across many closely spaced tones sent at once, so echoes do less damage. Wi-Fi and LTE use it.
Each bit is sent as one of two tones, and the pair of tones hops to a new frequency for every bit.
A 1 and a 0 are sent as two different tones.
A 1 and a 0 are sent as the same tone flipped upside down.
Sends two bits at a time as one of four phases of the same tone.
Sends bits by shifting the phase of a tone.
Sends several bits at once by changing both the strength and the phase of a tone.
How much stronger the signal is than the background noise, in dB.
A log scale for comparing power; every 10 dB is ten times the power.
A radio whose signal processing runs in software on a computer.
Turns a slice of signal into its list of frequencies.
Working on sound, radio or other signals as numbers in a computer.
How fast sound travels at each depth.
The fraction of bits that arrive wrong.
An equalizer that balances undoing the channel's echoes against boosting its noise.
Turns the level up or down on its own so the signal stays usable.
Echoes of one symbol spill into the next and blur them together.
A short check value sent with a message so the receiver can tell if any bits arrived wrong.
A feedback loop that keeps a receiver locked to the incoming signal's frequency and phase.
The small mismatch between the transmitter's and the receiver's radio frequencies.
A copy of the end of each OFDM symbol placed at its start, so echoes land there instead of in the next symbol.
A pulse shape for the symbols that keeps neighbors from blurring into each other.
The two parts, real and imaginary, that a radio splits a signal into.
The range of frequencies used for radio signals.
The side that sends.
The side that receives.
How many seconds until two vehicles would meet if nothing changes.
The standards body that defines the Basic Safety Message. (Its name began as the Society of Automotive Engineers.)
The U.S. Navy's science and technology research office.
A robot submarine that runs on its own, without a tether or a pilot.
Not an acronym. A NATO standard for underwater acoustic communication.
Not an acronym. A widely used program that traces sound paths through the ocean.
A survival swimming program for babies and young children.
A standards organization; its F2208 standard covers residential pool alarms. (Its name began as the American Society for Testing and Materials.)

The engineering department, and the field.

Sending a value as how long a repeating pulse stays on.
Turns a voltage into numbers a computer can use.
The circuit that drives a motor at the speed it's told.
The hobby radio link between a handheld transmitter and a receiver.
A wiring standard for sending digital audio between chips.
A way to send data over a network that doesn't wait to resend lost pieces, so it stays fast.

How many video frames arrive each second.
Software for drawing parts and assemblies in 3D.
The editing screen where a site's owner changes words and pictures without touching code.

Making a site easy for search engines to understand and rank.
The internet's directory that turns a web address into a server's location.
A defined way for one program to ask another for data or actions.
The language a web page's structure is written in.
The language that sets a web page's look: colors, fonts and layout.
A format for drawings made of lines and shapes that stay sharp at any size.
The standard checklist for making websites usable by people with disabilities.
Labels in a page's code that tell screen readers what each control is and does.
The browser's live tree of a page's elements.
The U.S. grid of townships, ranges and sections used to describe where land is.
The map file format Google Earth uses. A KMZ file is the zipped version.
The zipped form of a KML map file, the format Google Earth uses.
